subject: math
title: Grade 7 Financial Percentages: Discounts, GST and PST, Tips and Simple Interest
seo_title: Grade 7 Financial Percentages Worksheets: Discounts, GST + PST, Tips and Interest (Free, Answer Key, BC Curriculum)
meta_desc: Free Grade 7 math worksheets on financial percentages for the BC curriculum: percent of an amount, discounts and sale prices, 5% GST and 7% PST, tips, simple interest with I = Prt, best buys and budgets. 100 questions with an answer key, good FSA numeracy practice.
key_big: Write the percent as a decimal and multiply: 12% of $50 = $50 × 0.12 = $6.
key_sub: Take the discount first, then add the tax: 5% GST and 7% PST make 12% on most items in BC. Simple interest is I = Prt, with the rate as a decimal and the time in years.
body_html:
Percent of an amount

Percent means “out of 100”. To find a percent of an amount, write the percent as a decimal and multiply. 12% = 0.12, 5% = 0.05, 7% = 0.07.

You can also build percents from 10%: 10% is one tenth, 5% is half of 10%, and 1% is one hundredth.

Discounts and sale prices

A discount is a percent of the regular price. Subtract it, or multiply by what is left: 25% off means you pay 75%.

Example

An $80 jacket is 25% off. What is the sale price?

Discount: 25% of $80 = $20. Sale price: $80 − $20 = $60. Or: $80 × 0.75 = $60.

Answer: $60

Sales tax in BC: GST and PST

Most things you buy in BC have 5% GST and 7% PST added, 12% in total. Some items have only GST: children’s clothing and footwear, and restaurant meals. Find the sale price first, then add the tax.

Tips and simple interest

A tip is a percent of a restaurant bill, often 15% to 20% of the price before tax. Simple interest uses I = Prt: principal × yearly rate (as a decimal) × time in years.

Example

You save $500 at 3% simple interest per year for 2 years. How much is in the account?

I = $500 × 0.03 × 2 = $30. Balance: $500 + $30 = $530.

Answer: $530

Best buys and budgets

To find the best buy, compare the price for the same amount, such as per 100 g or per litre. When you plan a budget, remember to include the tax.

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
12% of $50 = $1212% = 0.12, so $50 × 0.12 = $6
25% off $60 = $60 − 25 = $35Find 25% of $60 ($15), then subtract: $45
Taking 25% off and adding 12% tax as one step: price × 0.87Take the discount first, then add 12% of the sale price
Adding PST to children’s clothing or restaurant mealsThese have 5% GST only
Using I = P × 3 × t for 3%Write the rate as a decimal: 3% = 0.03
Giving the interest as the balanceBalance = principal + interest

faq.q: What are GST and PST in BC?
faq.a: GST is the 5% federal sales tax and PST is BC’s 7% provincial sales tax, so most items have 12% added. Some items, like children’s clothing and restaurant meals, have only the 5% GST.

faq.q: How do you calculate a sale price with a percent discount?
faq.a: Find the percent of the regular price and subtract it, or multiply by the percent you still pay. For 25% off $80, the discount is $20 and the sale price is $60, the same as $80 × 0.75.

faq.q: How do Grade 7 students calculate simple interest?
faq.a: They use I = Prt: the principal times the yearly interest rate as a decimal times the time in years. $500 at 3% for 2 years earns $500 × 0.03 × 2 = $30.

faq.q: Do financial percent worksheets help with the Grade 7 FSA?
faq.a: Yes. The Grade 7 FSA includes numeracy, where students solve problems in real contexts. Working out discounts, sales tax, tips and interest is good practice for that kind of question.

items.q: What is 10% of $60?
items.e: 10% = 10 out of 100 = one tenth. $60 ÷ 10 = $6. ($50 subtracts 10 from 60; 10% is not $10.)

items.q: What is 50% of $37?
items.e: 50% is one half. $37 ÷ 2 = $18.50. ($7.40 divides by 5; $74 doubles instead of halving.)

items.q: What is 25% of $48?
What is 1% of $250?
What is 5% of $80?
items.e: 10% of $80 is $8, and 5% is half of that: $4. ($8 is 10%; $0.40 is 0.5%; $75 subtracts 5 from 80.)

items.q: What is 12% of $50?
items.e: 12% = 0.12. $50 × 0.12 = $6. Or: 10% is $5 and 2% is $1, so 12% is $6. ($12 uses the percent as dollars; $60 multiplies by 1.2 instead of 0.12.)

items.q: What is 15% of $40?
What is 20% of $85?
What is 7% of $30?
Which calculation finds 12% of a price?
items.e: Percent means “out of 100”, so 12% = 12 ÷ 100 = 0.12. Multiply: price × 0.12. price × 12 is 1200%, and price − 12 takes away $12, not 12%.

items.q: What is 75% of $36?
What is 30% of $45?
What is 5% of $64?
10% of $70 is $7. Use this to find 5% of $70.
items.e: 5% is half of 10%. $7 ÷ 2 = $3.50. ($14 doubles, which gives 20%; $0.70 is 1%.)

items.q: What is 12% of $25?
A $40 game is on sale. Chloe saves $10. What percent of the price does she save?
items.e: $10 out of $40 = 10/40 = 1/4 = 25%. (10% uses the dollars as the percent; 4% comes from 40 ÷ 10; 75% is the part paid.)

items.q: $9 is what percent of $60?
items.e: $9 ÷ $60 = 0.15 = 15%. Check: 10% of $60 is $6 and 5% is $3, so 15% is $9. (9% uses the dollars as the percent; 85% is the rest.)

items.q: What is 12% of $75?
What is 150% of $24?
What is 35% of $120?
A $40 sweater is 10% off. How much is the discount?
items.e: 10% of $40 = $40 ÷ 10 = $4 off. ($36 is the sale price, not the discount; $30 subtracts 10 from 40.)

items.q: A $40 sweater is 10% off. What is the sale price?
items.e: Discount: 10% of $40 = $4. Sale price: $40 − $4 = $36. ($30 subtracts the percent number, 10.)

items.q: What is the sale price of this rain jacket?
items.e: Discount: 25% of $60 = $60 ÷ 4 = $15. Sale price: $60 − $15 = $45. ($35 subtracts 25 dollars instead of 25%; $15 is the discount.)

items.q: An $80 pair of hiking boots is 50% off. What is the sale price?
items.e: 50% off is half off. $80 ÷ 2 = $40. ($30 subtracts 50 dollars; $79.50 subtracts 50¢; $120 adds 50%.)

items.q: A $35 board game is 20% off. What is the sale price?
items.e: Discount: 10% is $3.50, so 20% is $7. Sale price: $35 − $7 = $28. ($15 is 35 − 20; $7 is the discount.)

items.q: Which calculation gives the sale price when an item is 30% off?
items.e: 30% off means you pay 100% − 30% = 70% of the price, so price × 0.70. price × 0.30 gives only the discount.

items.q: What is the sale price of this snowboard?
A $48 soccer ball is 15% off. What is the sale price?
A $65 tent is 40% off. What is the sale price?
A $90 pair of skates is on sale for $72. What percent is the discount?
items.e: Discount: $90 − $72 = $18. Compare it with the regular price: $18 ÷ $90 = 0.2 = 20%. (18% uses the dollars; 80% is the part you pay; 25% divides by the sale price.)

items.q: A $50 pair of running shoes is on sale for $35. What percent is the discount?
items.e: Discount: $50 − $35 = $15. $15 ÷ $50 = 0.3 = 30%. (15% uses the dollars; 70% is the part you pay.)

items.q: A jacket costs $80. Store A takes 25% off. Store B takes $15 off. Which deal is better?
items.e: 25% of $80 = $20 off, so Store A’s price is $60. Store B’s price is $80 − $15 = $65. 25% off is better by $5. ($15 off by $10 compares 25 with 15, not dollars.)

items.q: A $28 T-shirt is on clearance for 75% off. What is the clearance price?
items.e: 25% of $28 is $7, so 75% off is $21 off. You pay 25%: $7. ($21 is the discount; $14 is 50% off.)

items.q: Two $18 T-shirts are on a deal: buy one, get the second one 50% off. How much do the two T-shirts cost before tax?
items.e: First T-shirt: $18. Second T-shirt: 50% of $18 off, so $9. Total: $18 + $9 = $27. ($36 forgets the discount.)

items.q: Olivia has $50. A $64 hoodie is 25% off. How much money does she have left after buying it (before tax)?
items.e: Sale price: 25% of $64 is $16, so $64 − $16 = $48. Left: $50 − $48 = $2. ($11 uses $64 − 25 = $39; $34 subtracts only the discount.)

items.q: A tent has a regular price of $120. It is on sale for $30 off. What percent off is that?
items.e: $30 ÷ $120 = 1/4 = 25%. (30% uses the dollars; 4% comes from 120 ÷ 30; 75% is the part you pay.)

items.q: A $100 winter coat is 20% off. Then the store takes another 10% off the sale price. What is the final price?
items.e: 20% off: $100 − $20 = $80. Another 10% off $80: $80 − $8 = $72. ($70 adds the percents to 30%, but the second 10% is taken from $80, not $100.)

items.q: Is 20% off and then another 10% off the same as 30% off?
c: No, it is 28% off in total
No, it is 32% off in total
No, it is 2% off in total
items.e: On $100: 20% off gives $80, then 10% of $80 is $8 off, so the price is $72. That is $28 off $100: 28% off in total. The second discount is taken from a smaller price.

items.q: A pair of ski goggles is 25% off. The sale price is $45. What was the regular price?
items.e: The sale price is 75% of the regular price. 75% is $45, so 25% is $45 ÷ 3 = $15, and 100% is 4 × $15 = $60. Check: 25% of $60 is $15 and $60 − $15 = $45. ($56.25 adds 25% of $45 instead.)

items.q: Store A sells a jacket for $85 at 20% off. Store B sells the same jacket for $75 at 10% off. Which store has the lower price?
items.e: Store A: 20% of $85 is $17, so $85 − $17 = $68.00. Store B: 10% of $75 is $7.50, so $75 − $7.50 = $67.50. Store B is lower, at $67.50. ($65.00 subtracts the percent numbers as dollars.)

items.q: In BC, most things you buy have 5% GST and 7% PST added. What percent is added in total?
items.e: Add the two tax rates: 5% + 7% = 12%. So on most items you pay 12¢ more for every $1.

items.q: A $40 lamp has 5% GST added. How much is the GST?
A $40 lamp has 7% PST added. How much is the PST?
items.e: 7% = 0.07. $40 × 0.07 = $2.80. ($7 uses the percent as dollars; $28 multiplies by 0.7.)

items.q: A $50 pair of headphones has 5% GST and 7% PST added. How much tax is that in total?
A $50 pair of headphones has 12% tax added (5% GST + 7% PST). What is the total price?
Which calculation gives the total price of an item with 5% GST and 7% PST added?
items.e: The total is 100% of the price plus 12% tax = 112% = 1.12. So price × 1.12. price × 0.12 gives only the tax.

items.q: In BC, which item has 5% GST but no PST?
items.e: Children’s clothing and footwear have no PST in BC, so a child’s winter jacket has only 5% GST. The other items have both GST and PST (12%).

items.q: A pair of children’s rain boots costs $30. Children’s footwear has 5% GST but no PST. What is the total price?
items.e: Only GST applies: $30 × 0.05 = $1.50. Total: $30 + $1.50 = $31.50. ($33.60 adds 12%, but there is no PST.)

items.q: A family’s restaurant meal costs $24 before tax. Restaurant meals in BC have 5% GST but no PST. What is the total?
items.e: GST: $24 × 0.05 = $1.20. Total: $24 + $1.20 = $25.20. ($26.88 adds 12%, but restaurant food has no PST.)

items.q: A $70 video game has 5% GST and 7% PST added. What is the total price?
An $85 skateboard has 5% GST and 7% PST added. What is the total price?
What is the total on this receipt?
items.e: Add the subtotal and both taxes: $45.00 + $2.25 + $3.15 = $50.40. ($47.25 forgets the PST; $57 adds $12.)

items.q: A pair of earbuds costs $24.99. How much is the 7% PST, rounded to the nearest cent?
items.e: $24.99 × 0.07 = $1.7493, which rounds to $1.75. (Do not just cut off the digits; $17.49 multiplies by 0.7; $2.99 is 12%, both taxes.)

items.q: The $24.99 earbuds have 5% GST and 7% PST added. What is the total price?
A $16 board game has 5% GST and 7% PST added. Mateo pays with cash. How much does he pay?
items.e: Tax: $16 × 0.12 = $1.92. Total: $17.92. Canada has no pennies, so a cash total rounds to the nearest 5¢: $17.92 → $17.90. ($17.92 is what a card pays.)

items.q: About how much GST and PST is added to an adult jacket that costs $39.99? Round the price first.
items.e: $39.99 is about $40. 12% of $40: 10% is $4 and 2% is $0.80, so about $4.80. ($12 adds 12 dollars; $2 is only the 5% GST.)

items.q: A total of $67.20 includes 5% GST and 7% PST. What was the price before tax?
items.e: The total is 112% of the price, so price × 1.12 = $67.20. Price = $67.20 ÷ 1.12 = $60. Check: $60 × 1.12 = $67.20. ($59.14 takes 12% of the total, but the tax was 12% of the price.)

items.q: A pair of $80 headphones is 25% off. Then 5% GST and 7% PST are added. What is the total?
items.e: Sale price: $80 − $20 = $60. Tax: 12% of $60 = $7.20. Total: $60 + $7.20 = $67.20. (Do not subtract 25% and add 12% in one step: $80 × 0.87 = $69.60 is wrong, because the tax is on the sale price. $72 adds $12.)

items.q: A $50 item has a $10-off coupon. The 12% tax (GST + PST) is charged on the price after the coupon. What is the total?
items.e: Coupon first: $50 − $10 = $40. Tax: 12% of $40 = $4.80. Total: $44.80. ($46 adds the tax before taking off the coupon: $56 − $10. Tax is charged on the price you actually pay.)

items.q: A child’s T-shirt costs $15 (5% GST only). An adult hoodie costs $40 (5% GST and 7% PST). What is the total for both?
A restaurant bill is $40. How much is a 15% tip?
items.e: 10% of $40 is $4 and 5% is $2. 15% = $4 + $2 = $6. ($15 uses the percent as dollars; $4 is only 10%.)

items.q: A pizza delivery costs $35. How much is a 20% tip?
A meal costs $50. How much is an 18% tip?
items.e: $50 × 0.18 = $9. Or: 10% is $5, 8% is $4, and $5 + $4 = $9. ($18 uses the percent as dollars.)

items.q: A $60 meal has a 15% tip added. What is the total with the tip (before tax)?
10% of a $46 bill is $4.60. Use this to find a 15% tip.
Simran and 3 friends share a $48 pizza order. They add a 20% tip and split the total equally. How much does each person pay?
items.e: Tip: 20% of $48 = $9.60. Total: $57.60. 4 people: $57.60 ÷ 4 = $14.40. ($12 forgets the tip; $57.60 is the whole bill.)

items.q: The simple interest formula is I = Prt. What does r stand for?
c: The interest rate per year, as a decimal
The total amount at the end
items.e: I is the interest, P is the principal (starting amount), r is the yearly interest rate written as a decimal (3% = 0.03), and t is the time in years.

items.q: What is the simple interest on $200 at 3% per year for 1 year?
items.e: I = Prt = $200 × 0.03 × 1 = $6. ($600 uses 3 instead of 0.03; $206 is the balance, not the interest.)

items.q: What is the simple interest on $500 at 2% per year for 3 years?
items.e: I = Prt = $500 × 0.02 × 3 = $10 × 3 = $30. ($10 is only 1 year; $3000 uses 2 instead of 0.02; $530 is the balance.)

items.q: Leah puts $400 in a savings account that pays 4% simple interest per year. How much is in the account after 2 years?
items.e: I = $400 × 0.04 × 2 = $32. Balance: $400 + $32 = $432. ($32 is only the interest; $416 is after 1 year.)

items.q: What is the simple interest on $1000 at 1.5% per year for 4 years?
Which earns more simple interest: $300 at 2% per year for 5 years, or $500 at 1% per year for 3 years?
items.e: $300 × 0.02 × 5 = $30. $500 × 0.01 × 3 = $15. The $300 for 5 years earns $15 more. A bigger principal does not always earn more; the rate and the time matter too.

items.q: $800 earns $24 of simple interest in 1 year. What is the interest rate?
$600 earns 2% simple interest per year. How many years until it earns $36 of interest?
items.e: Interest each year: $600 × 0.02 = $12. $36 ÷ $12 = 3 years. (18 divides $36 by 2; 12 is the interest for one year, not the time.)

items.q: Zara borrows $250 for a new phone at 8% simple interest per year. How much must she pay back after 1 year?
items.e: I = $250 × 0.08 × 1 = $20. Pay back: $250 + $20 = $270. ($20 is only the interest; $258 adds $8; $2250 uses 8 instead of 0.08.)

items.q: What is the simple interest on $1200 at 3% per year for 6 months?
items.e: 6 months is half a year, so t = 0.5. I = $1200 × 0.03 × 0.5 = $36 × 0.5 = $18. ($36 is a full year; $216 uses t = 6.)

items.q: Liam’s family has a $40 restaurant meal. 5% GST is added (no PST on restaurant food), and they tip 15% of the price before tax. How much do they pay in total?
items.e: GST: $40 × 0.05 = $2. Tip: 15% of $40 = $6. Total: $40 + $2 + $6 = $48. ($42 forgets the tip; $46 forgets the GST; $48.30 takes the tip on the taxed amount.)

items.q: Hana puts $350 into a savings account at 2% simple interest per year for 2 years. What is the balance at the end?
items.e: I = $350 × 0.02 × 2 = $14. Balance: $350 + $14 = $364. ($14 is the interest; $357 is after 1 year; $1750 uses 2 instead of 0.02.)

items.q: How much more is a 20% tip than a 15% tip on a $64 bill?
items.e: The difference is 5% of $64 = $3.20. (Check: 20% is $12.80 and 15% is $9.60; $12.80 − $9.60 = $3.20.) ($5 uses the percents as dollars.)

items.q: How much must you put in a savings account at 3% simple interest per year to earn $45 in 1 year?
Which bag of granola is the better buy?
c: Both cost the same per 100 g
items.e: Compare the price per 100 g, not the total price. Bag A: $4.50 ÷ 5 = $0.90 per 100 g; Bag B: $6.80 ÷ 8 = $0.85 per 100 g. Bag B has the lowest price per 100 g, so it is the best buy. (Bag A has the lowest total, but you get less.)

items.q: Which jug of apple juice is the best buy?
c: They all cost the same per litre
items.e: Compare the price per litre, not the total price. Jug A: $2.40 ÷ 1 = $2.40 per litre; Jug B: $4.40 ÷ 2 = $2.20 per litre; Jug C: $9.20 ÷ 4 = $2.30 per litre. Jug B has the lowest price per litre, so it is the best buy. (Jug A has the lowest total, but you get less.)

items.q: A 600 g piece of wild BC salmon costs $13.20. What is the price per kilogram?
items.e: 1 kg = 1000 g, and 600 g = 0.6 kg. $13.20 ÷ 0.6 = $22.00 per kilogram. Check: 0.6 × $22 = $13.20. ($7.92 multiplies by 0.6; $2.20 is the price per 100 g.)

items.q: The community pool charges $7 per swim, or $90 for a 15-swim pass. Noah plans to swim 15 times. Which is cheaper, and by how much?
items.e: Paying each swim: 15 × $7 = $105. The pass: $90. $105 − $90 = $15, so the pass is cheaper by $15. ($83 is $90 − $7.)

items.q: A $60 pair of adult running shoes is 20% off. 5% GST and 7% PST are added to the sale price. What is the total?
items.e: Sale price: $60 − $12 = $48. Tax: 12% of $48 = $5.76. Total: $48 + $5.76 = $53.76. ($55.20 combines 20% off and 12% tax into 8% off; $48 forgets the tax.)

items.q: Lucas earns $15 an hour babysitting and works 6 hours. He spends 40% and saves the rest. How much does he save?
What percent of Wei’s money in goes to savings?
items.e: Money in: $50 + $30 = $80. Savings: $24. $24 ÷ $80 = 0.3 = 30%. (24% uses the dollars; 40% compares savings with spending, $24 ÷ $60.)

items.q: Mei wants a $250 snowboard for the winter. 5% GST and 7% PST are added. She has $40 saved and saves $25 a week. How many more weeks until she can buy it?
items.e: Total: $250 × 1.12 = $280. Still needed: $280 − $40 = $240. $240 ÷ $25 = 9.6, so round up to 10 weeks. (9 weeks forgets the tax or rounds down; 12 weeks forgets the $40 saved; 11 weeks also rounds down.)

items.q: Arjun puts $600 from a summer job into a savings account at 2.5% simple interest per year. How much interest does he earn in 2 years?
Headphones cost $90. One coupon gives 30% off. Another gives $25 off. What is the lower price before tax?
items.e: 30% off: 30% of $90 = $27, so $63. $25 off: $65. The lower price is $63. ($60 subtracts 30 dollars; $70.56 adds the tax.)

items.q: Emma and 3 friends have dinner in Vancouver. The food costs $72. 5% GST is added (no PST on restaurant food), and they tip 18% of the price before tax. They split the total equally. How much does each person pay?
items.e: GST: $72 × 0.05 = $3.60. Tip: $72 × 0.18 = $12.96. Total: $72 + $3.60 + $12.96 = $88.56. Each: $88.56 ÷ 4 = $22.14. ($18.90 forgets the tip; $23.40 adds PST, which restaurant food does not have.)

items.q: Which bag of rice is the better buy?
c: Both cost the same per kilogram
items.e: Compare the price per kilogram, not the total price. Bag A: $7.80 ÷ 2 = $3.90 per kilogram; Bag B: $18.50 ÷ 5 = $3.70 per kilogram. Bag B has the lowest price per kilogram, so it is the best buy. (Bag A has the lowest total, but you get less.)

items.q: Owen earns $240 picking fruit in the Okanagan. He plans to save 50%, spend 30% and give 20% to charity. How much will he give?
Last year a school raised $1250 at its Terry Fox Run. This year it raised 20% more. How much did it raise this year?
A hockey registration fee of $400 goes up by 5% next season. What is the new fee?
items.e: 5% of $400 = $20. New fee: $400 + $20 = $420. ($405 adds $5; $380 subtracts the increase.)

items.q: Store A sells a speaker for $50 plus 12% tax (GST + PST). Store B sells the same speaker for $55 with tax included. Which is cheaper?
items.e: Store A: $50 × 1.12 = $56. Store B: $55. Store B is cheaper by $1. (Store A by $5 forgets to add the tax to Store A’s price.)

items.q: Ji-woo borrows $300 from her parents for a bike and agrees to pay 5% simple interest per year. She pays it all back after 2 years. How much does she pay back?
items.e: I = $300 × 0.05 × 2 = $30. Pay back: $300 + $30 = $330. ($315 is only 1 year of interest; $30 is only the interest.)

items.q: At a café in Victoria, Jasleen buys lunch for $11.40. 5% GST is added (no PST on food). She pays cash with a $20 bill. How much change does she get?
items.e: GST: $11.40 × 0.05 = $0.57. Total: $11.97. Cash rounds to the nearest 5¢: $11.95. Change: $20.00 − $11.95 = $8.05. ($8.03 forgets the cash rounding; $8.60 forgets the GST; $7.25 adds PST too.)

items.q: Ethan has $100 in his bank account. He buys a $90 adult rain jacket at 20% off, and 5% GST and 7% PST are added. He pays by debit. How much is left in the account?
items.e: Sale price: $90 − $18 = $72. Tax: 12% of $72 = $8.64. Total: $80.64. Left: $100.00 − $80.64 = $19.36. Debit is exact, so there is no rounding. ($28 forgets the tax; $17.20 combines 20% off and 12% tax into 8% off.)

items.q: A soccer team buys 4 adult jerseys at $30 each. The store gives 10% off the whole order, then adds 5% GST and 7% PST. What is the total?
items.e: Before the discount: 4 × $30 = $120. 10% off: $120 − $12 = $108. Tax: 12% of $108 = $12.96. Total: $108 + $12.96 = $120.96. ($108 forgets the tax; $134.40 forgets the discount; $122.40 is $120 × 1.02, which combines 10% off and 12% tax.)
